_rules: The price argument — no tour contracts, no middlemen — is OWNED BY THE HOMEPAGE's Why Lucky section (HANDOFF §7) and is deliberately not re-argued here. This page is about who Lucky is, not why it is cheap. No underdog story and no manifesto about disrupting golf, per the tone guide.
_blocked: Photography. Every image on this page is a labelled brief. Cole also sent two visual references for this page that were never described into HANDOFF and the screenshots are gone (§3) — the rows below are built from what is verifiable, so those references can be applied later without restructuring the page.
headline: We built the clubs we wanted
lede: Lucky Golf makes forged wedges, CNC-milled putters and a titanium hybrid, in gold, at prices that surprise people. There is no origin myth here. Somebody thought these clubs should exist, so they got made.

hero.brief: 21:9. The line together on turf — wedge, putter, hybrid — early light, gold reading warm rather than yellow. No hands, no model.

stats.headline: Numbers anyone can look up

items.v: Customers, and more than 10,000 orders. Shopify's count, not an estimate.
Reviews across the club line on Judge.me, averaging 4.78.
Clubs in the bag today: two wedge finishes, two putters, one hybrid.

stats.note: Every one of these is checkable. That is the only reason they are on the page.

rows.title: Real materials, and nothing hidden behind them
rows.phBrief: 4:3 macro. A milled wedge face, raking light across the grooves so the sandblast texture reads. Close enough to see the machining.
paras: The wedges are forged from 1020 carbon steel with a milled and sandblasted face. The putters are cut from a single block of stainless — 431 in the blade, 304 in the mallet. The hybrid is titanium with a flex-channel face.

None of that is unusual for a good club. What is unusual is publishing it plainly, per loft, in a table you can read before you buy, including the rows where we do not have a number yet. If a spec is missing from this site it is because nobody has measured it, not because it is inconvenient.

rows.title: Sixty days, because you cannot judge a wedge in a shop
rows.phBrief: 4:3. A golfer mid-round with a Lucky wedge, shot from behind at address. Course context, not studio. Natural light.
paras: Every club gets sixty days. Roll the putter. Hit one wedge on a mat. If it does not earn a place in the bag, tell us and send it back.
The conditions are specific and they are on the returns page in full, because a sixty-day promise with the catches buried is not really a sixty-day promise.

rows.title: A small company, and it shows in the good way
rows.phBrief: 4:3. Cole, working — packing an order or on the phone, in the space where it actually happens. Not a posed headshot.
paras: The inbox is read by people who handle the clubs. When an order goes missing, the person sorting it out is usually the person who sold it to you.

That is not a service promise with a number attached — there isn't one published, and inventing one would be worse than admitting it. It is just what the reviews describe, over and over, in customers' own words.

quote.text: I ordered a Christmas present for my boyfriend, it got lost in the mail. Cole personally texted me to get the correct information, and sent a new one that arrived a few days later. I highly recommend!!
quote.note: Verbatim from Judge.me, like every quote on this site. Nothing here is written by us and attributed to somebody else.

close.headline: The clubs are the argument
close.body: Everything above is context. The reason to buy a Lucky wedge is the wedge, and there are sixty days to decide whether that holds up.
